title: Part 2, Chapter 12
paragraphs: The strange adventure that befell the valiant Don Quixote with the bold Knight of the Mirrors

Don Quixote and his squire spent the night following their encounter with Death under some tall, shady trees, and at Sancho’s urging Don Quixote ate a little from the provisions Dapple carried. Over their supper Sancho said to his master, “Señor, what a fool I would have looked if I had chosen the spoils of the first adventure your worship accomplished as my reward, instead of the foals of the three mares. It just goes to show: ‘a sparrow in the hand is better than a vulture on the wing.’”

“Even so, Sancho,” Don Quixote replied, “if you had let me attack them as I wanted to, you would have come away with at least the emperor’s gold crown and Cupid’s painted wings as plunder, for I would have taken them by force and placed them in your hands.”
“The scepters and crowns of those play-actor emperors,” said Sancho, “were never solid gold — only brass foil or tin.”

“True enough,” said Don Quixote, “for it would hardly be right for the props of a play to be real instead of mere fictions and appearances, like the play itself. And toward the drama, Sancho — and, by necessary extension, toward those who perform and produce it — I would have you kindly disposed, for they are all instruments of great good to the State, holding up to us at every turn a mirror in which the doings of human life are vividly displayed; and no comparison shows us more faithfully what we are and what we ought to be than the play and the players. Come, tell me: have you never seen a play performed in which kings, emperors, pontiffs, knights, ladies, and assorted other characters appear? One plays the villain, another the rogue, this one the merchant, that one the soldier, one the quick-witted fool, another the foolish lover; and when the play is over and they take off the costumes they wore in it, all the actors are equal again.”
“Yes, I have seen plays like that,” said Sancho.

“Well then,” said Don Quixote, “the very same thing happens in the comedy and the life of this world, where some play emperors, others popes — in short, every character that can be brought onto a stage; but when it is over, that is to say, when life ends, death strips them all of the costumes that set one apart from another, and in the grave they are all equal.”

“A fine comparison!” said Sancho, “though not so new that I haven’t heard it many, many times — like that other one about the game of chess: as long as the game lasts, each piece has its own particular role, and when the game is finished they are all mixed up, jumbled together, and shaken into the bag, which is a good deal like ending life in the grave.”
“Every day, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “you grow less of a dolt and more of a wit.”

“Ay,” said Sancho, “some of your worship’s shrewdness must be rubbing off on me. Land that is barren and dry by nature will come to bear good fruit if you manure it and work it; what I mean is that your worship’s conversation has been the manure spread on the barren soil of my dry wit, and all the time I have spent in your service and your company has been the tilling; and with that help I hope to bear fruit in abundance — fruit that won’t fall off or slip away from those paths of good breeding your worship has worn into my parched understanding.”

Don Quixote laughed at Sancho’s high-flown phrasing, but he saw that what Sancho said about his own improvement was true, for every so often he spoke in a way that astonished him — though always, or almost always, when Sancho tried to talk grandly and reach for polished language, he ended by tumbling from the heights of his simplicity into the depths of his ignorance. Where he showed his polish and his memory to best advantage was in hauling in proverbs, whether or not they had any bearing on the matter at hand, as has been seen already and will be noticed again in the course of this history.

They passed a good part of the night in talk of this kind, but at last Sancho felt the urge to let down the curtains of his eyes, as he liked to say when he wanted to go to sleep; and after unloading Dapple he turned him loose to graze his fill. He did not remove Rocinante’s saddle, because his master’s express orders were that as long as they were in the field, or not sleeping under a roof, Rocinante was not to be stripped — for the ancient custom established and observed by knights-errant was to take off the bridle and hang it on the saddlebow, but to remove the saddle from the horse? Never! So Sancho did exactly that, and gave Rocinante the same liberty he had given Dapple. The friendship between those two animals was so rare and so strong that tradition, handed down from father to son, holds that the author of this truthful history devoted special chapters to it, which, to preserve the propriety and dignity owed to so heroic a history, he left out — though now and then he forgets that resolve and describes how eagerly the two beasts would scratch each other when they were together, and how, when they were tired or had eaten their fill, Rocinante would lay his neck across Dapple’s — it stretched half a yard or more out the other side — and the pair would stand like that, gazing thoughtfully at the ground, for three days, or at least for as long as they were left alone or hunger did not drive them off in search of food. I may add that the author is said to have left it on record that he compared their friendship to that of Nisus and Euryalus, and of Pylades and Orestes; and if that is so, the whole world may admire how firm the friendship of these two peaceable animals must have been — to the shame of men, who keep their friendships with one another so poorly. That is why it was said—

Friend is no longer friend to friend;
The reeds turn into lances now.
And another has sung—
Friend to friend, the bug — and so on.

And let no one suppose the author was off the mark in comparing the friendship of these animals to the friendship of men; for men have taken many lessons from beasts and learned many important things from them — for example, the clyster from the stork, vomiting and gratitude from the dog, vigilance from the crane, foresight from the ant, modesty from the elephant, and loyalty from the horse.

Sancho finally fell asleep at the foot of a cork tree, while Don Quixote dozed at the foot of a sturdy oak; but only a short while had passed when a noise behind him woke him. Starting up, he listened and peered in the direction the sound came from, and made out two men on horseback, one of whom slid down from the saddle and said to the other, “Dismount, my friend, and take the bridles off the horses; as far as I can see, this place will supply grass enough for them, and the solitude and silence my lovesick thoughts require.” As he said this he stretched himself out on the ground, and the armor he wore clattered as he threw himself down — a clear sign, to Don Quixote, that he must be a knight-errant. So he went over to the sleeping Sancho, shook him by the arm, brought him back to his senses with no small effort, and said to him in a low voice, “Brother Sancho, we have an adventure.”
“God send us a good one,” said Sancho; “and where might her ladyship the adventure be?”

“Where, Sancho?” replied Don Quixote. “Turn your eyes and look, and you will see a knight-errant stretched out over there — one who, it strikes me, is not particularly happy, for I saw him fling himself off his horse and throw himself on the ground with a certain air of dejection, and his armor rattled as he fell.”
“And how does your worship figure that makes it an adventure?” said Sancho.

“I do not claim,” Don Quixote answered, “that it is a complete adventure, only the beginning of one — for this is how adventures begin. But listen: it seems he is tuning a lute or a guitar, and from the way he is spitting and clearing his throat he must be getting ready to sing something.”
“My word, you’re right,” said Sancho; “he must be some knight in love.”

“There is no knight-errant who isn’t,” said Don Quixote. “But let us listen to him, for if he sings, by that thread we shall draw out the ball of his thoughts — because out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”

Sancho was about to answer his master, but the voice of the Knight of the Grove — which was neither very bad nor very good — cut him short, and listening attentively the two of them heard him sing this
A Sonnet

Declare your pleasure, lady mine, I pray;
Set down the terms that I am bound to keep;
I shape my will submissively to yours,
And from your law my feet shall never stray.
Would you have me die, mute prey to grief?
Then count me here and now as dead and cold;
Would you have me tell my woes some novel way?
Then Love itself shall be the one to tell my tale.
I am made the proof of opposites in union,
Fashioned of soft wax and of hard diamond both;
And yet, obedient to the laws of love,
I offer you my breast here, hard or soft:
Whatever you engrave or stamp upon it
Shall rest indelible for all eternity.

With an “Ah me!” that seemed dragged from the deepest recesses of his heart, the Knight of the Grove brought his song to an end, and a moment later he cried out in a mournful, pitiful voice, “O fairest and most ungrateful woman on earth! How can it be, most serene Casildea de Vandalia, that you allow this captive knight of yours to wear himself out and perish in endless wanderings and harsh, grinding labors? Is it not enough that I have compelled all the knights of Navarre, all the Leonese, all the Tartesians, all the Castilians, and finally all the knights of La Mancha, to confess you the most beautiful woman in the world?”

“Not so,” said Don Quixote at this, “for I am of La Mancha, and I have never confessed any such thing; I neither could nor should confess anything so damaging to my lady’s beauty. You can see, Sancho, that this knight is raving. But let us keep listening; perhaps he will tell us more about himself.”
“That he will,” returned Sancho, “for he looks to be in the mood to keep lamenting for a month at a stretch.”

But it did not turn out that way, for the Knight of the Grove, hearing voices close by, broke off his lamentation, rose to his feet, and called out in a clear but courteous tone, “Who goes there? What sort of people are you? Do you count yourselves among the happy or among the miserable?”
“Among the miserable,” answered Don Quixote.
“Then come to me,” said the Knight of the Grove, “and be assured that you are coming to sorrow itself and affliction itself.”
Finding himself answered so gently and courteously, Don Quixote went over to him, and Sancho did the same.

The mournful knight took Don Quixote by the arm and said, “Sit down here, sir knight; for proof that you are one, and one of those who profess knight-errantry, it is enough for me to have found you in this place, where solitude and night — the natural couch and proper retreat of knights-errant — keep you company.” To which Don Quixote answered, “A knight I am, and of the profession you name; and though sorrows, misfortunes, and calamities have made their home in my heart, the compassion I feel for the misfortunes of others has not been driven out of it. From what you sang just now I gather that your troubles spring from love — I mean, from the love you bear that beautiful ingrate you named in your lament.”
Meanwhile they had settled down together on the hard ground, peaceful and companionable, just as if at daybreak they were not going to crack each other’s skulls.
“Might you, sir knight, happen to be in love?” the Knight of the Grove asked Don Quixote.
“By mischance I am,” replied Don Quixote; “though the pains that come from well-placed affections ought to be counted as favors rather than misfortunes.”
“True,” returned the Knight of the Grove, “provided scorn does not unsettle our reason and understanding; for when scorn is excessive, it looks more like revenge.”
“My lady has never scorned me,” said Don Quixote.
“Certainly not,” said Sancho, who stood close by, “for my lady is gentle as a lamb and softer than a roll of butter.”
“Is this your squire?” asked the Knight of the Grove.
“He is indeed,” said Don Quixote.

“I have never yet seen a squire,” said the Knight of the Grove, “who dared to speak while his master was speaking; there is mine, at any rate — as big a man as his father — and no one can prove he has ever opened his lips while I am talking.”
“Well, by my faith,” said Sancho, “I have spoken, and I am fit to speak, in front of a man as much, or even — but never mind; the more you stir it, the worse it gets.”

The squire of the Grove took Sancho by the arm and said to him, “Let the two of us go off where we can talk squire-fashion to our hearts’ content, and leave these gentlemen our masters to fight it out over the stories of their loves; you may be sure daybreak will find them still at it, nowhere near finished.”
“By all means, let’s,” said Sancho; “and I will tell your worship who I am, so that you can judge whether or not I deserve a place among the most talkative squires going.”
With that the two squires drew off to one side, and the conversation that passed between them was every bit as comical as the one between their masters was solemn.
